45.t: Taxi (jitney) dances and the Levita job band
45.s: Williams explains jitney dances, a nickel a dance, and recalls Lewis Givens, Raymond Brown and others in the band.
45.ch: Taxi dance job and the Fiesta
45.q: I don't know whether he played any white dances or not, but I know he played quite a few colored. Like them balls you see they'd hide. Yeah, nice band. The La Vida, by the way, what was that? I never didn't understand what that was. Taxi dancing. You would have taxi dances. Yeah, Jitney, huh?…

45.t: Hours, ticket rules and closing of the taxi dance hall
45.s: Pay was good but the hours brutal; musicians played two choruses a dance, patrons bought tickets, and the hall was shut during the war over watered-down drinks.
45.ch: Taxi dance job and the Fiesta
45.q: Worked for me at that time. Yeah. 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, you know. It was good pay. Oh, yeah. It was good pay, but Lord, hours.

300.t: Moving to the Astoria and the Sunday jitney dance
300.s: Humphrey describes the Astoria job, pay of about $78, and the suburban jitney dance at La Vida.
300.q: I didn't wake there for two years. And then, we got to the poppy, you know, and come and sign us at the Astor, you know? Rene was waking at the Astor until, you know, Sunday night until 12 o'clock. Then, we take over at 12.30, you know, after our dance, make $78. Mm-hmm. Got poppy there, and he had…

300.t: How the ticket-based taxi dance worked
300.s: Humphrey explains the dance-hall ticket system, dime dances and how the girls were paid, and the two-year job.
300.q: Yeah, sure, man, they give them a salary and then plus the percentage off the tickets. They, they take one piece and turn into the ticket taker. Well, now when they add up, put, put all them in the envelope, check in to the, when they go to get paid off, now how many dancing in the middle of the…

474.s: The tickets, short dances, waltzes, leaders and the matron.
474.q: They said five minutes dance but it was uh two minutes you know. And they were they snatched tickets you know. Mmhmm. They danced. And they played the waltz. And I played with uh people like Handi was on that job. He stayed there a long time. Allison was the leader one time. Allison went to the…

268.t: Working conditions and pay at La Vida taxi dance hall
268.s: The job ran nonstop; pay was low during the Depression with ten cents a dance. The hostesses worked on percentage.
268.ch: Entertainers, Creole Serenaders and La Vida
268.q: They had other little jobs opening, you know, but that was about one of the best regular jobs, you see. Regular, that's the man thing. They wasn't paying but two fifteen at night, yeah. Did you make much tips? Not there. Ten cents a dance, you know.

875.t: Taxi-dance halls: hostesses, tickets and patrons
875.s: Howard describes how dance-hall girls were paid by ticket split, that the halls were all white, who the patrons were, and the slow numbers.
875.q: Over at the dance hall? Yeah, like the Vito. Well they have maybe about 25 or so like that. And they got, I think they, I'm quite sure they got half of the ticket. See, the guys come up to the ticket box and they buy it and they think you gotta give it to the girl. Yeah, every dance. Every dance,…

404.t: San Jacinto badges, later presidents and Mitchell as treasurer
404.s: Members wore metal badges and got into dances free; after Monette, Webber took over and Mitchell was treasurer.
404.q: after monette uh let's see we had uh uh i think webber took over edmund webber yeah yeah zizi zizi well they were on seminar street yeah well he took it over because he was running things for for beans and that's yeah yeah made him be manager yeah the time of the the club part man i i worked the…

84.t: Getting the La Vida job; the music and hours
84.s: He tells how he got La Vida when the pianist quit, lists personnel, and describes a waltz every fourth number.
84.q: I was playing there with a fellow by the name of Tink. Piano player. Tink's been there, oh, in quite a number of years. Tink was that Tink? Yeah, but, uh... Yeah.

715.t: Freelancing and the dance school job: fatigue and ticket dancing
715.s: Allen describes gigging with different bands and a current taxi dance hall job: tiring four-piece nights, slow numbers, and tickets four for a dollar.
715.q: Yeah, pretty good shape if I don't have to work too hard. I have a job for a safe instrument and a hard job to play with a big band. I don't think I can live now. Where I get four or five bands I got to pound out of it.

641.t: Taxi dance halls: Liberty and the One-Eleven
641.s: Joe describes the downtown taxi-dance halls, with Tudie's band at One-Eleven, and how dime tickets split with the dancing girls.
641.ch: Los Angeles with Mutt Carey and the taxi dances
641.q: It was on East Third Street in downtown Los Angeles, the Liberty Dance Hall. And at 111 West Third Street, right across Main Street... That was the dividing line between east and west.

232.s: Fields explains the ten-cents-a-dance system and paying bands on percentage.
232.ch: Tulsa bands, Trent, Holder and Kirk
232.q: What it was is you would go into a place and the guy would tell you that you've got to do so many dances an hour, to figure out the money he's going to make, and it's ten cents a dance. You've got to be on your P's and Q's. If I remember right, I believe no dance could be over three minutes.
